transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you into the clinic today?

Hi, yeah, um... well, it's a bit of a long story, but I guess I'm here because I've started doing these... things, at work and at school, that just really do not make any sense at all. I work as a bookkeeping clerk, mostly handling accounts and expense reports, and lately, instead of just doing my job, my behavior has been getting really strange. 

Like, the other day at the office, I had this massive stack of receipts to process. Normally I just enter them straight into the software, but instead, I found myself getting down on my hands and knees and lining them all up, edge to edge, all the way across the floor of the office. I didn't even really know why I was doing it, it just happened. And then with my calculator—since I'm crunching numbers all day—I've started tapping the keys in these exact sets of nine. Always nine. I'll just sit there tapping the plastic over and over in nines instead of actually doing the math for the accounts. 

But I think the thing that really made me realize I needed to come in, or at least made my boss pull me aside, was what happened by the copier. I went over to make copies of some invoices, but I didn't use the machine. I just... stood there. I raised both my hands up in the air, kind of like I was being robbed or something, and I just froze like that. I just stood by the copier with my hands held up in the air for I don't even know how long, completely stuck, just waiting until one of my coworkers finally walked by and asked if I was okay. It's just really embarrassing and confusing, because I'm 22, I'm trying to do well at my job and keep up with my classes, but I keep doing these weird things that I can't explain.
When you find yourself tapping the keys in nines or lining up the receipts, is there a specific fear or thought driving you to do it, or does it just happen without any clear reason?

Well, it's... it's not just random, even though I know it probably looks completely random to everyone else in the office. When I'm doing the tapping, or when I was on the floor with those receipts, it’s because of the numbers themselves. You see, working as a bookkeeping clerk, I am looking at literally hundreds of numbers every single day. It’s just a constant stream of data coming across my desk. But lately, I’ve been looking at them, and... I know it sounds really strange to say out loud, but I get completely convinced that certain invoice totals, specific account numbers, and even the due dates on the billing statements aren't just regular business expenses. I get this overwhelming feeling that they are actual messages, specifically about me. 

Like, if an invoice total has a certain sequence, or a due date lines up with an account number in a specific way, it feels like a code that’s been placed there on purpose. That's why I was tapping the nines, I was trying to respond to it, or figure it out. And it gets so frustrating because it takes up so much of my time, and I'll actually take these invoices to my supervisor—he's been there forever, really patient guy—and I'll try to show him what I'm seeing. He will literally sit down with me at his computer, pull up the vendor files, and show me the original purchase orders to prove that they are just completely normal entries. He walks me through the whole paper trail to show me it's just regular office supplies or utility bills. 

But the thing is, even after he does all that, and I see the proof right there on the screen... I still can't shake it. I go back to my desk and I still feel like they are tracking me. Like whoever is putting these numbers into the system is watching me to see whether I understand the pattern they're laying out. So I end up lining up the receipts because I feel like if I can just get them all laid out edge to edge, I'll finally be able to see the whole message and prove that I get the pattern. I just get so wrapped up in it, even when part of my brain knows it's just an expense report, the other part is just screaming that I'm being tested.
Do you have any diagnosed medical conditions or ongoing physical health problems?

No, I don't. I mean, physically, I'm totally fine. I don't have asthma, I don't have diabetes, no heart stuff, nothing like that. I've never even really broken a bone or had surgery, except for when I got my wisdom teeth out in high school, but I don't think that counts, right? That's just a normal thing. But yeah, as far as actual medical conditions, I don't have any. I try to take decent care of myself, you know, I eat okay, I try to get enough sleep when my brain isn't keeping me up with all the numbers and the patterns. 

Actually, I did go to my regular doctor a few months ago for a physical, just a standard check-up because my mom was bugging me about it, and my blood pressure was totally normal, my blood work was all clear. He said I was perfectly healthy. So it's not like there's some physical illness making me do all this stuff at work. It's just... whatever is going on in my head. But physically? No, I'm completely healthy. I don't take any regular medications for anything physical, either. Just vitamins sometimes, if I remember to buy them. But yeah, no ongoing health problems at all.
You mentioned freezing with your hands in the air by the copier—has that kind of freezing or holding a posture happened at other times?

Well, yeah, that's... that's exactly it. That's why I'm here, really, because it's not just the copier. I mean, the copier was the most embarrassing one, obviously, because the whole office could basically see me just standing there like a statue, but it's part of this whole... this whole thing where I'm just doing things that completely don't make any sense. At work, at school, it's like my body just does these weird things. 

Like I was saying before, the freezing is just one part of it. The other stuff, the lining up the receipts all the way across the floor... I mean, who does that? I'm supposed to be a bookkeeping clerk, I'm supposed to be entering data, and instead I'm on the carpet making this massive paper trail. And the tapping the calculator, the sets of nine, over and over and over. It's like I get stuck. Whether it's my hands stuck in the air by the Xerox machine, or my finger stuck hitting the 'nine' key, or me stuck on the floor with the expense reports... it's all just this bizarre behavior that I can't explain to anyone, not even to myself. And it's happening more and more, which is why I finally decided I had to come in and talk to someone, because standing by the copier with my hands up like I'm surrendering to an invisible bank robber until Susan from HR has to ask if I'm having a stroke... it's just not normal. It really doesn't make any sense at all.

Well, it's funny you ask that, because... yeah, actually. I do. And it's really unsettling, to be honest. It's not like a constant chatter or anything, but sometimes, especially when I'm alone, it happens. Like, if I'm just sitting at my desk at work, you know, it's late in the afternoon, maybe most people have gone home or they're in a meeting, and it's just me and the hum of the fluorescent lights and the computer fan. Or even when I'm walking home from my evening classes, just walking down the sidewalk, totally by myself. 

Out of nowhere, I'll hear this voice. It's a man's voice, very distinct, very clear. It doesn't sound like it's inside my head, it sounds like someone is standing right behind me or just over my shoulder. And he'll say these really specific things. He'll say, 'Check line seven,' or 'You missed the sign.' And it's so clear, so incredibly real, that I physically turn around. I literally stop what I'm doing, whether I'm typing in an invoice or walking past the corner store, and I look behind me. I scan the whole area, expecting to see some guy standing there in a suit or something, looking at my paperwork. But there's never anyone there. It's just empty space. 

And then my heart starts racing, because I know I heard it. I know I did. It's not a mumble, it's not the wind. It's a direct instruction. 'Check line seven.' And of course, because of everything else going on with the numbers and the patterns I was telling you about, when I hear that, I immediately go back to my spreadsheet and look at line seven. And I'll stare at it for twenty minutes, trying to figure out what he meant, what I missed. It just feeds right into that whole feeling that I'm being tested or guided by someone I can't see. It's exhausting, really, because I can't just ignore it when it sounds that real. I just can't.

Well, if I really sit down and trace it all back, it hasn't been happening forever, you know? It’s not like I’ve always been like this. It’s really been building up for, I’d say, about ten months now. 

Ten months ago was right around the time I decided I needed to get more serious about my future. Because, you know, I’m a bookkeeping clerk right now, but I only have my high school diploma, and I realized pretty quickly that if I ever want to move up or make real money, I need actual qualifications. So, I enrolled in these evening accounting courses. I figured I could handle it, right? 

But that meant I was keeping my full-time bookkeeping job during the day—which is already just staring at screens and numbers and ledgers for eight hours—and then I’d rush straight over to the campus for these night classes. And that’s exactly when all of this started. At first, I just thought I was exhausted. You know, burning the candle at both ends, staring at spreadsheets all day and then textbooks all night. I figured my brain was just tired. But then the numbers started feeling... different. And then the tapping started, and the freezing up, and eventually that voice telling me to check the lines. 

It didn't all happen overnight, it just sort of snowballed over these last ten months since I started the classes. It’s like my brain never gets a break from the data, whether I’m at the office or sitting at a desk at school, and the whole thing just kept escalating until I ended up standing by the copier like a mannequin. So yeah, about ten months of this just slowly taking over everything.

Well, it's funny you ask that, because... no, not really. I mean, I don't think so. It's not like I try to speak and the words won't come out, or like my throat is paralyzed or anything. It's more like... I just don't have anything to say in that exact moment. Or maybe I'm just so focused on whatever is happening, like the freezing or the numbers, that talking isn't even on my radar. 

Like with the copier incident, right? When Susan from HR came over and asked if I was having a stroke. I could hear her perfectly fine. I knew exactly what she was saying, and I knew it was a ridiculous situation. But I didn't say, 'Help, I can't move,' or 'No, Susan, I'm fine, just stuck.' I just sort of... stood there. I think I eventually mumbled something like 'just thinking' once I snapped out of it, but during the actual freeze? No, I wasn't talking. But I don't think it was because I *couldn't* talk, you know? It's just that the whole system was on pause. 

It's the same when I'm tapping the calculator. If someone walks by and says, 'Hey, you got those expense reports done?' I might not answer right away, because I have to finish the set of nine. If I interrupt the set of nine to say, 'Yeah, they're almost done,' then the whole sequence is ruined and I have to start over. So I just stay quiet until I'm finished. People probably think I'm ignoring them or being rude, or maybe they think I'm just incredibly absorbed in my work, which, I guess, I am, in a weird way. But it's not that I'm physically incapable of speaking. It's just that speaking would disrupt the pattern, or break the freeze, and for some reason, in that moment, the pattern or the freeze feels like the most important thing in the world. So, no, I wouldn't say I *can't* speak. I just... don't.

I mean... I don't really know, to be honest. Because no one has actually ever tried to do that. It’s not like I’m surrounded by people who just walk up and start rearranging my arms, you know? I work in a pretty typical office environment, and people are very... hands-off. It’s all about personal space. 

Like, going back to that time with Susan from HR by the copier—she was definitely freaked out, and she came kind of close, leaning in to look at my face, but she didn’t actually touch me. She didn’t poke my shoulder or grab my arm or try to move me out of the way. I think people are just too polite, or maybe they’re just really uncomfortable when someone is acting out of the ordinary, so they keep their distance. They might wave a hand a few feet away, but physical contact? No. 

And even when I’m at home, if I get stuck while I'm studying for my night classes—which happens sometimes when I'm sitting at the kitchen table with my accounting textbooks spread out everywhere—my roommate is usually just in his room playing video games. If he comes out to get a glass of water and sees me just staring blankly at a page, he just kind of ignores it. He probably just thinks I'm zoning out really hard on tax law or just completely exhausted from working all day. He's definitely not the type to come over and try to pose me. 

So, I’ve never actually been in a situation where someone tried to physically move me or bend my elbow or change my posture while I’m in one of those frozen states. I honestly have no idea what would happen. I don't know if my arm would just stay exactly where they put it, or if my muscles would be completely stiff like a board, or if someone grabbing me would be the exact thing that finally snaps me out of the freeze. It’s a good question, really, but yeah... I just don't have an answer for you because nobody’s ever laid a finger on me during one of those moments.

Well... no. Frantic? No, definitely not. Honestly, I don’t think I even have the energy for anything that you could call frantic physical activity. 

I mean, if you just think about my day-to-day schedule right now, it’s basically the exact opposite of frantic. I’m sitting in an office chair—which they claim is ergonomic, but my lower back would strongly disagree with that—staring at dual monitors for eight hours straight, just processing invoices and reconciling accounts. And then I get in my car, sit in traffic for forty-five minutes, and go sit in a lecture hall for another three hours. So my body is mostly just... entirely stationary. I'm practically glued to a chair from the moment I wake up until I go to sleep.

The absolute closest thing to physical activity I have going on with all this weird stuff is the tapping I mentioned earlier. But that’s not frantic at all. It’s actually very, very deliberate. It's controlled. When I tap the calculator keys or the edge of my desk, it’s not like I’m flailing my arms around or pacing the room or jumping out of my skin. It’s a very specific, measured rhythm. It has to be in those sets of nine, like I said, and it has to be perfect. If I were frantic or flailing around, I'd mess up the count, and then I'd have to start the whole sequence over, which is incredibly frustrating. So the tapping requires focus, not frantic energy.

Sometimes I do feel a lot of tension, sure, like this really tight, wound-up coil in my chest from all the stress of the classes and the numbers not looking right, and of course that voice chiming in. But that tension never explodes into me running around or moving wildly. If anything, the stress just makes me freeze up more, like we were just talking about with the copier. All that pressure builds up and instead of making me hyper or frantic, I just kind of power down physically. I just stop. So, yeah, no sudden bursts of running around or moving frantically. It's really just the opposite. I just sit there, or I freeze.

Well, it's funny you ask that, because... no, not really. I mean, I don't think so. It's not like I try to speak and the words won't come out, or like my throat is paralyzed or anything. It's more like... I just don't have anything to say in that exact moment. Or maybe I'm just so focused on whatever is happening, like the freezing or the numbers, that talking isn't even on my radar. 

Like with the copier incident, right? When Susan from HR came over and asked if I was having a stroke. I could hear her perfectly fine. I knew exactly what she was saying, and I knew it was a ridiculous situation. But I didn't say, 'Help, I can't move,' or 'No, Susan, I'm fine, just stuck.' I just sort of... stood there. I think I eventually mumbled something like 'just thinking' once I snapped out of it, but during the actual freeze? No, I wasn't talking. But I don't think it was because I *couldn't* talk, you know? It's just that the whole system was on pause. 

It's the same when I'm tapping the calculator. If someone walks by and says, 'Hey, you got those expense reports done?' I might not answer right away, because I have to finish the set of nine. If I interrupt the set of nine to say, 'Yeah, they're almost done,' then the whole sequence is ruined and I have to start over. So I just stay quiet until I'm finished. People probably think I'm ignoring them or being rude, or maybe they think I'm just incredibly absorbed in my work, which, I guess, I am, in a weird way. But it's not that I'm physically incapable of speaking. It's just that speaking would disrupt the pattern, or break the freeze, and for some reason, in that moment, the pattern or the freeze feels like the most important thing in the world. So, no, I wouldn't say I *can't* speak. I just... don't.

doctor.question: {"intent": "Assess for waxy flexibility or rigidity to evaluate for catatonic schizophrenia.", "question": "If someone tries to move your arms or change your posture when you are frozen, do your limbs

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about waxy flexibility or rigidity (if limbs stay in place when moved by someone else during a freezing episode), which is not explicitly detailed in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I mean... I don't really know, to be honest. Because no one has actually ever tried to do that. It’s not like I’m surrounded by people who just walk up and start rearranging my arms, you know? I work in a pretty typical office environment, and people are very... hands-off. It’s all about personal space. 

Like, going back to that time with Susan from HR by the copier—she was definitely freaked out, and she came kind of close, leaning in to look at my face, but she didn’t actually touch me. She didn’t poke my shoulder or grab my arm or try to move me out of the way. I think people are just too polite, or maybe they’re just really uncomfortable when someone is acting out of the ordinary, so they keep their distance. They might wave a hand a few feet away, but physical contact? No. 

And even when I’m at home, if I get stuck while I'm studying for my night classes—which happens sometimes when I'm sitting at the kitchen table with my accounting textbooks spread out everywhere—my roommate is usually just in his room playing video games. If he comes out to get a glass of water and sees me just staring blankly at a page, he just kind of ignores it. He probably just thinks I'm zoning out really hard on tax law or just completely exhausted from working all day. He's definitely not the type to come over and try to pose me. 

So, I’ve never actually been in a situation where someone tried to physically move me or bend my elbow or change my posture while I’m in one of those frozen states. I honestly have no idea what would happen. I don't know if my arm would just stay exactly where they put it, or if my muscles would be completely stiff like a board, or if someone grabbing me would be the exact thing that finally snaps me out of the freeze. It’s a good question, really, but yeah... I just don't have an answer for you because nobody’s ever laid a finger on me during one of those moments.

doctor.question: {"intent": "Assess for catatonic excitement or purposeless agitation to evaluate whether catatonic symptoms dominate the clinical picture.", "question": "Have you ever experienced sudden episodes of intense, frantic physical

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about catatonic excitement or sudden episodes of intense, frantic physical agitation. The patient's profile does not include this specific symptom (their disorganized/catatonic behavior involves freezing, tapping, and lining up receipts, but not frantic physical excitement).

patient.answer:
Well... no. Frantic? No, definitely not. Honestly, I don’t think I even have the energy for anything that you could call frantic physical activity. 

I mean, if you just think about my day-to-day schedule right now, it’s basically the exact opposite of frantic. I’m sitting in an office chair—which they claim is ergonomic, but my lower back would strongly disagree with that—staring at dual monitors for eight hours straight, just processing invoices and reconciling accounts. And then I get in my car, sit in traffic for forty-five minutes, and go sit in a lecture hall for another three hours. So my body is mostly just... entirely stationary. I'm practically glued to a chair from the moment I wake up until I go to sleep.

The absolute closest thing to physical activity I have going on with all this weird stuff is the tapping I mentioned earlier. But that’s not frantic at all. It’s actually very, very deliberate. It's controlled. When I tap the calculator keys or the edge of my desk, it’s not like I’m flailing my arms around or pacing the room or jumping out of my skin. It’s a very specific, measured rhythm. It has to be in those sets of nine, like I said, and it has to be perfect. If I were frantic or flailing around, I'd mess up the count, and then I'd have to start the whole sequence over, which is incredibly frustrating. So the tapping requires focus, not frantic energy.

Sometimes I do feel a lot of tension, sure, like this really tight, wound-up coil in my chest from all the stress of the classes and the numbers not looking right, and of course that voice chiming in. But that tension never explodes into me running around or moving wildly. If anything, the stress just makes me freeze up more, like we were just talking about with the copier. All that pressure builds up and instead of making me hyper or frantic, I just kind of power down physically. I just stop. So, yeah, no sudden bursts of running around or moving frantically. It's really just the opposite. I just sit there, or I freeze.
